```{r setup, include=FALSE}

# !Kung San adults (Howell): our running example
howell <- load_howell() |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      if_else(male == 1, "male", "female"),
      levels = c("female", "male")
    ),
    z_height = standardize(height),
    z_weight = standardize(weight)
  )

h_mean <- mean(howell$height)
h_sd <- sd(howell$height)
w_mean <- mean(howell$weight)
w_sd <- sd(howell$weight)
r_hw <- cor(howell$height, howell$weight)
h_women <- mean(howell$height[howell$male == 0])
h_men <- mean(howell$height[howell$male == 1])
spreads <- two_spreads(howell)
sex_fit <- sex_weight_fits(howell)

houses <- load_houses() |>
  mutate(z_price = standardize(price), z_area = standardize(area_m2))
```

# The average pilot {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#average-pilot"}

_Around 1950, US Air Force pilots kept losing control of their planes._

- [The cockpits had been designed in 1926 to fit the **average pilot**.]{.fragment}
- [So the Air Force measured 4,063 pilots on the ten body sizes that matter most in a
  cockpit: height, chest, arm length…]{.fragment}
- [How many were close to average (the middle 30%) on all ten?]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment .stat-reveal}
[0]{.stat-number} [[out of 4,063 pilots]{.stat-caption}]{.stat-captions .fragment}
:::

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
The fix: adjustable seats.\
Design for the distribution, not the average.
:::

[Gilbert S. Daniels, *The "Average Man"?* (Wright Air Development Center, 1952); retold
in Todd Rose, *The End of Average* (2016).]{.source}

# You already think in distributions {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#commute"}

::: {.exchange}
[_"How long is your trip here?"_]{.exchange-q} [_"Usually 30 minutes."_]{.exchange-a .fragment}
:::

::: {.kinds}
::: {.kind .kind-population .fragment}
[_"Usually"_]{.kind-title}

Not every trip: some take 20 minutes, some 45.

How trips **vary**: a [population distribution]{.blue}.
:::

::: {.kind .kind-certainty .fragment}
[_"How do you know?"_]{.kind-title}

You've made the trip a hundred times. A newcomer couldn't be so sure.

How **sure** you are: a [certainty distribution]{.green}.
:::

::: {.kind .kind-correlative .fragment}
[_"What if it rains?"_]{.kind-title}

Rain, traffic, the hour you leave: each one shifts the whole spread.

How it changes **with** something else: a [correlative distribution]{.orange}.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
You already think in distributions.\
This week, we draw them.
:::

# This week's goals {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#goals"}

- [Learn three ways to think with distributions:]{.fragment}
  - [**Population**]{.blue}: how cases vary
  - [**Certainty**]{.green}: how sure we are
  - [**Correlative**]{.orange}: how two things vary together
- [See why adding one variable to a model changes what the others mean]{.fragment}
- [Work through an example: what makes a house expensive?]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment}
A distribution is a different way to think about a number: [every value it could take,
and how common or plausible each one is]{.blue}.
:::


# Part 1: Population distributions {.center .part-1 notes="notes/week2_notes.md#part1"}

{{< include _includes/week2/three-kinds.md >}}

# Random individuals, predictable crowds {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#galton"}

_At every peg, a ball bounces left or right: a coin flip. Drop some balls._

{{< include _includes/week2/galton.md >}}

::: {.fragment}
One ball: anyone's guess. A thousand balls: [the same shape, every time]{.blue}.
:::

## A shape tells a story {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#nepal-population"}

## Our running example: the !Kung San {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#kung"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Census data collected by anthropologist **Nancy Howell** in the late 1960s among
  the !Kung San of the Kalahari.
- `r nrow(howell)` adults (18+).
- Height (cm), weight (kg), age, sex.
- The same data McElreath uses in *Statistical Rethinking*.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r howell-table}
howell |>
  select(height, weight, age, sex) |>
  head(6) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```
:::
:::

```{r kung-data}
kung_widget_data(howell) # for the widgets later in the deck
```

## Center, spread, shape {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#describing"}

```{r height-hist}
height_hist_plot(howell)
```

- [**Center**]{.red}: where is a typical value? (the mean)
- [**Spread**]{.blue}: how far is a typical case from the center? (the standard deviation)
- **Shape**: one hump or two? Symmetric, or a long tail?

## One hump or two? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#two-humps"}

_The !Kung heights are two crowds, not one._

```{r height-sex, fig.height = 5.4}
height_sex_plot(howell)
```

::: {.fragment}
Women average `r fmt(h_women)` cm, men `r fmt(h_men)` cm. But the crowds overlap: [plenty
of women are taller than plenty of men]{.blue}. (Hold on to this. It comes back.)
:::

## The Normal distribution {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#normal"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r normal-overlay}
normal_overlay_plot(howell)
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
The blue curve is a Normal distribution with the same center and spread as the data:

- mean = `r fmt(h_mean)` cm
- SD = `r fmt(h_sd)` cm

::: {.fragment}
**Two numbers** describe the whole shape.

Real data are never perfectly Normal, but many things come close. Like the Galton
board: many small, random pushes add up to a bell.
:::
:::
:::

## The 68–95–99.7 rule {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#rule-68-95"}

```{r normal-rule, fig.height = 5.5}
normal_rule_plot()
```

- For a Normal distribution, about **68%** of cases fall within 1 SD of the mean, and
  **95%** within 2 SD.
- [Check: `r fmt(100 * mean(abs(howell$z_height) < 1), 0)`% of !Kung adults are within
  1 SD of the average height, and `r fmt(100 * mean(abs(howell$z_height) < 2), 0)`%
  within 2 SD.]{.fragment}

## Taller or heavier? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#z-scores"}

```{r z-example}
ex_h <- 165
ex_w <- 58
ex_zh <- (ex_h - h_mean) / h_sd
ex_zw <- (ex_w - w_mean) / w_sd
```

_A !Kung man is **`r ex_h` cm** tall and weighs **`r ex_w` kg**. Is he more unusually
tall, or more unusually heavy?_

- We can't compare centimeters to kilograms.
- [But we can ask of each: **how many standard deviations from average is this?**]{.fragment fragment-index=1}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
$$
z = \frac{x - \text{mean}}{\text{SD}}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Height: (`r ex_h` − `r fmt(h_mean)`) / `r fmt(h_sd)` = [**`r fmt(ex_zh, 2)`**]{.blue}
- Weight: (`r ex_w` − `r fmt(w_mean)`) / `r fmt(w_sd)` = [**`r fmt(ex_zw, 2)`**]{.red}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
He is more unusually heavy than he is tall. A **z-score** says where one case sits in
the crowd.
:::

## Same data, new ruler {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#new-ruler"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r hist-cm, opts.label = "half_short"}
height_ruler_plot(howell)
```
:::

::: {.column}
```{r hist-z, opts.label = "half_short"}
height_ruler_plot(howell, z = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

- The **shape** doesn't change at all. Only the labels on the axis.
- The mean becomes **0**. The standard deviation becomes **1**.
- The units disappear: a z-score is measured in "standard deviations".

## Reading z-scores {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#reading-z"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| z      | Meaning                          |
|--------|----------------------------------|
| 0      | exactly average                  |
| ±1     | ordinary                         |
| ±2     | unusual (about 1 in 20)          |
| ±3     | rare (about 1 in 370)            |
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
In R:

```{r z-code, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
howell |>
  mutate(
    z_height = (height - mean(height)) / sd(height),
    z_weight = (weight - mean(weight)) / sd(weight)
  )
```
:::
:::

z-scores compare things measured on different scales: exam marks out of 50 and out of
100, rupees and dollars, centimeters and kilograms.

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
An average describes the crowd.\
The distribution describes everyone in it.
:::


# Part 2: Certainty distributions {.center .part-2 notes="notes/week2_notes.md#part2"}

{{< include _includes/week2/three-kinds.md >}}

# How old is he? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#belief-distributions"}

_One man, one true age. The only thing that varies is how sure we are._

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.small-caption}
**Uninformed** I have no idea. He could be between 0 and 100 and I don't think any possibility is more likely than any other.
:::
```{r belief-uninformed, opts.label = "belief"}
belief_plot(function(x) dunif(x, 0, 100))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.small-caption}
**Weakly informed** He seems like he's about 40, but I could be very wrong about that. Anything between 20 and 60 seems plausible and even more extreme values are possible.
:::
```{r belief-weak, opts.label = "belief"}
belief_plot(function(x) dnorm(x, 40, 15), ymax = 0.1)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/week2/man.png){height="550px" fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.small-caption}
**Strongly informed** I'm quite certain that he's forty or relatively close to it.
:::
```{r belief-strong, opts.label = "belief"}
belief_plot(function(x) dnorm(x, 40, 1))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.small-caption}
**Domain-specific** I'm fairly sure he's between 30 and 50, but I have no idea where in that range he lands. Older or younger than that seems unlikely, though.
:::
```{r belief-domain, opts.label = "belief"}
belief_plot(plateau_density(center = 40, plateau = 20, taper = 15), ymax = 0.05)
```
:::
:::

:::

## How sure can a few people make us? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#sample-mean"}

_Pretend these `r nrow(howell)` adults are everyone. We can only afford to measure a few._

{{< include _includes/week2/sample-mean.md >}}

## Two spreads {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#two-spreads"}

_If we measured n adults, from a much bigger population:_

| Adults measured | [Most adults are within]{.blue} | [95% sure the average is within]{.green} |
|--:|--:|--:|
| `r spreads$n[1]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[1])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[1])` cm |
| `r spreads$n[2]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[2])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[2])` cm |
| `r spreads$n[3]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[3])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[3])` cm |
| `r spreads$n[4]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[4])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[4])` cm |

::: {.fragment}
More data doesn't make people any less different. [It makes us more sure.]{.green}
:::

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
Variation is in the world.\
Uncertainty is in us.
:::

## Population or certainty? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#two-kinds"}

::: {.kinds}
::: {.kind .kind-population}
[Population distributions]{.kind-title}

How a quantity **varies across cases**. Many cases, each with its own value.

- Heights of the adults in a village
- Prices of houses sold last year
- Ages of everyone in Nepal
:::

::: {.kind .kind-certainty}
[Certainty distributions]{.kind-title}

How **plausible** each value of an unknown is. One true value; we're unsure which.

- The mayor's share of the vote (Week 1)
- The age of the man in the photo
- The average height of all !Kung adults
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Quick test: [many cases that really differ]{.blue}, or [one answer we're unsure
about]{.green}? Same shapes, same vocabulary, different questions.
:::


# Part 3: Correlative distributions {.center .part-3 notes="notes/week2_notes.md#part3"}

{{< include _includes/week2/three-kinds.md >}}

# Two variables at once {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#correlation"}

```{r scatter-raw, fig.height = 5.8}
ggplot(howell, aes(height, weight)) +
  geom_point(color = ORANGE, alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)", y = "Weight (kg)")
```

- Height and weight each have their own [population distribution]{.blue}. The
  scatterplot shows them **together**: each dot is one adult.
- [Taller people tend to be heavier. But what does "tend to" look like?]{.fragment}

## A relationship is a distribution that moves {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#conditional"}

_Pick a height. How do the weights of adults that tall vary?_

{{< include _includes/week2/conditional.md >}}

::: {.fragment}
That's [P( weight | height )]{.orange}: Week 1's bar, for a whole distribution.
:::

## Standardize both variables {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#standardize-both"}

_Each adult votes: on the same side of average for both, or on opposite sides?_

```{r scatter-z, fig.height = 6}
agreement_plot(howell)
```

## Correlation is average agreement {.mechanics notes="notes/week2_notes.md#average-agreement"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
$$
r = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{\text{height},i} \times z_{\text{weight},i}
$$

- Each person "votes":
  - [Same side of average on both → **positive** vote]{.blue}
  - [Opposite sides → **negative** vote]{.red}
- *r* is the average vote.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r cor-code, echo = TRUE}
cor(howell$height, howell$weight)
```

- *r* is always between **−1** and **+1**.
- *r* has no units.
- Standardizing changes nothing: *r* in cm/kg = *r* in z-scores.
:::
:::

## What does *r* look like? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#r-gallery"}

```{r cor-gallery, fig.height = 3.6}
cor_gallery_plot()
```

- Our height and weight: *r* = `r fmt(r_hw, 2)`. A strong relationship, but far from perfect.
- [*r* = 0.3 looks like almost nothing. Many published papers report less.]{.fragment}

## What correlation misses {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#cor-misses"}

```{r cor-misses, fig.height = 5.5}
cor_misses_plot()
```

- *r* only measures **straight-line** agreement.
- [**Always plot your data** before trusting a single number.]{.fragment}

## Regression: our first coefficient {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#regression"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r candidate-lines, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5}
candidate_lines_plot(howell, r_hw)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
A line through the middle of the moving distribution. In z-scores, both variables have
mean 0, so the line needs only **one number**: its slope, β.

$$
z_{\text{weight}} = \beta \times z_{\text{height}}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Which line describes the data best?
:::
:::
:::

## The best line {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#best-line"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r residuals, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5}
residuals_plot(howell, r_hw)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- The [red lines]{.red} are the **misses**: how far each person is from the line.
- The best line makes the misses as small as possible overall.
- [With standardized data and one predictor, the best β is exactly the correlation:
  **β = r = `r fmt(r_hw, 2)`**.]{.fragment}
:::
:::

## Reading the coefficient {.mechanics notes="notes/week2_notes.md#reading-coef"}

```{r slope-units}
slope_kg_cm <- r_hw * w_sd / h_sd
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- In z-scores: **β = `r fmt(r_hw, 2)`**
  - "An adult 1 SD taller than average is, on average, `r fmt(r_hw, 2)` SD heavier."
- Back in real units: β × SD~weight~ / SD~height~
  - `r fmt(r_hw, 2)` × `r fmt(w_sd)` / `r fmt(h_sd)` = **`r fmt(slope_kg_cm, 2)` kg per cm**
  - "Each extra centimeter of height goes with about `r fmt(slope_kg_cm, 2)` kg more
    weight."
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r slope-plot, opts.label = "half"}
ggplot(howell, aes(height, weight)) +
  geom_point(color = GRAY, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = ORANGE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)", y = "Weight (kg)")
```

```{r lm-code, echo = TRUE}
coef(lm(weight ~ height, data = howell))
```
:::
:::

## How sure are we about β? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#beta-posterior"}

```{r beta-posterior, fig.height = 5.5}
beta_posterior_plot(howell)
```

- β is a number we don't know, so it gets a [certainty distribution]{.green}: prior ×
  likelihood → posterior, like the mayor's vote share last week.
- [With 20 adults we're unsure about β. With `r nrow(howell)`, much less so.]{.fragment}

## A headline from pure noise {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#noise"}

```{r noise-sim}
# 50 made-up "indicators" for 20 made-up "countries", all pure random noise
set.seed(3)
n_vars <- 50
noise_small <- matrix(rnorm(20 * n_vars), nrow = 20)
r_small <- cor(noise_small)
r_small[lower.tri(r_small, diag = TRUE)] <- NA
best <- which(abs(r_small) == max(abs(r_small), na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)
r_best <- r_small[best]
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r noise-best, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
tibble(x = noise_small[, best[1]], y = noise_small[, best[2]]) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = ORANGE, size = 4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = RED, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = paste("Variable", best[1]), y = paste("Variable", best[2]))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
> _"Countries that spend more on [one thing] have `r if (r_best > 0) "more" else "less"`
> [another]"_ (*r* = `r fmt(r_best, 2)`)

::: {.fragment}
- I made up `r n_vars` variables for 20 "countries", every value drawn at random:
  nothing is related to anything.
- That's `r choose(n_vars, 2)` possible pairs. This is the strongest.
- Give these two variables names, and it's a headline.
:::
:::
:::

## How much *r* varies by chance {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#small-samples"}

```{r noise-dist, fig.height = 5}
noise_dist_plot(r_small, n_vars)
```

- Each histogram shows how much *r* varies by chance alone, when nothing is going on.
  With [20 cases]{.green}, chance alone produces values of ±0.5 and beyond. With
  [500 cases]{.green}, they stay close to 0.
- [It's Week 1's problem again: search enough pairs, and some will look "significant."
  A wide certainty distribution is the honest answer: _"I'm not sure yet."_]{.fragment}

# Do men weigh more? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#sex-weight"}

_Back to the two crowds from Part 1._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r sex-weight, opts.label = "half_tall"}
sex_weight_plot(howell)
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
- Women average `r fmt(sex_fit$weight_women)` kg, men `r fmt(sex_fit$weight_men)` kg.
- [Fit weight on sex alone, and the coefficient for sex is [**+`r fmt(sex_fit$total)`
  kg**]{.orange}.]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment}
Is that because they're men, or because they're taller?
:::
:::
:::

## Compare adults of the same height {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#same-height"}

_Pick a height. Compare only the women and men that tall._

{{< include _includes/week2/conditional-sex.md >}}

## Add height, and sex stops predicting weight {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#sex-height"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
|  | weight ~ sex | [weight ~ sex + height]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |
|---|--:|--:|
| **Sex** (men − women) | [+`r fmt(sex_fit$total)` kg]{.orange} | [[`r fmt(sex_fit$direct)` kg]{.orange}]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |
| **Height** (per cm) |  | [+`r fmt(sex_fit$slope, 2)` kg]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
Men are `r fmt(sex_fit$height_gap)` cm taller. At `r fmt(sex_fit$slope, 2)` kg per cm:\
`r fmt(sex_fit$height_gap)` × `r fmt(sex_fit$slope, 2)` = [**`r fmt(sex_fit$height_gap * sex_fit$slope)` kg**]{.orange}.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
The effect of sex on weight passes **through height**. The direct effect is about zero
(somewhere between `r fmt(sex_fit$direct_lo)` and +`r fmt(sex_fit$direct_hi)` kg).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
```{r sex-dag, opts.label = "dag_half"}
sex_path_dag()
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4 .big-statement}
Adding one variable changed the answer for another.
:::

## Which number is right? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#which-right"}

_Both. They answer different questions._

| Question | Model | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| Do men weigh more than women? | weight ~ sex | Yes: [`r fmt(sex_fit$total)` kg more]{.orange} |
| Do men weigh more than women [of the same height]{.blue}? | weight ~ sex + height | No: [about the same]{.orange} |

- [A coefficient's meaning depends on what else is in the model.]{.fragment}
- [Add a variable, and it can change, vanish or even flip. You'll see a flip in the
  house prices.]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
The data can't tell us which question to ask.\
That's next week.
:::


# Summary: three ways to think with distributions {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#summary"}

A **distribution** is a different way to think about a number: every value it could
take, and how common or plausible each one is.

::: {.kinds}
::: {.kind .kind-population}
[Population]{.kind-title}

How cases vary: center, spread and shape. A z-score places one case.

An average describes the crowd, not anyone in it.
:::

::: {.kind .kind-certainty}
[Certainty]{.kind-title}

How sure we are about something we don't know. Wide when we know little, narrow with
more data.

Variation is in the world. Uncertainty is in us.
:::

::: {.kind .kind-correlative}
[Correlative]{.kind-title}

How one distribution moves with something else: *r* and β.

A coefficient's meaning depends on what else is in the model.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
Think in distributions, not single numbers.
:::

# Next week {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#next-week"}

- Correlation and regression describe **how** things vary together. They don't say
  **why**.
- Adding height made sex's coefficient vanish. Adding living area will flip bedrooms'.
  Which models answer the questions we care about?
- [The data can't decide. We have to say what we think causes what: **DAGs** and
  **causal models**, next week.]{.fragment}

| Week | Topic | Punchline |
|:-:|---|---|
| 1 | Updating | Do science, not statistics. |
| **2** | **Distributions** | **Change how you think about numbers.** |
| 3 | Models | Draw your assumptions and make them explicit. |
| 4 | Confounders | Look behind every pattern. |
| 5 | Interpretation | Ask what's missing and what's hidden. |


# Practical work: What makes a house expensive? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses"}

_Appendix: we'll work through this together with the TA in our second session._

All three kinds of distribution, on real data:

- **The question**: which features of a house go with a higher price, and how much?
- **The data**: `r fmt(nrow(houses), 0)` house sales in Ames, a US college town.
- **The tools**: a [population distribution]{.blue} of prices, [correlative
  distributions]{.orange} of price with each feature, and [certainty
  distributions]{.green} for each coefficient.

::: {.callout-note title="A deliberately simple model"}
Straight lines, one coefficient per feature. No neighborhoods, no house condition, no
year of sale. We'll add the thinking behind those choices next week.
:::

## The data: house sales in Ames, Iowa {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-data"}

- `r fmt(nrow(houses), 0)` houses sold 2006–2010 in Ames, a US college town
  (De Cock, 2011). Prices in US dollars; areas converted to m².

```{r houses-table}
houses |>
  select(price, area_m2, year_built, bedrooms, bathrooms, garage_cars) |>
  head(6) |>
  mutate(price = dollars(price)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "r")
```

## Step 1: The distribution of prices {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-step1"}

```{r price-hist, fig.height = 5.5}
price_hist_plot(houses)
```

- Not Normal: a **long right tail** of a few very expensive houses.
- The tail pulls the [mean]{.red} above the [median]{.blue}. Which is the "typical" price?

## Step 2: How unusual is this house? {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-step2"}

```{r unusual-houses}
unusual <- bind_rows(
  houses |> slice_max(price, n = 1) |> mutate(house = "A: most expensive"),
  houses |> slice_max(area_m2, n = 1) |> mutate(house = "B: largest")
)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| | Mean | SD |
|-|------|----|
| Price | `r dollars(mean(houses$price))` | `r dollars(sd(houses$price))` |
| Living area | `r fmt(mean(houses$area_m2))` m² | `r fmt(sd(houses$area_m2))` m² |
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r unusual-table}
unusual |>
  transmute(house, price = dollars(price), `area (m²)` = area_m2) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```
:::
:::

**Your turn:** compute the z-scores for houses A and B. Which one is more unusual, and
in what way?

::: {.fragment}
```{r unusual-z}
unusual |>
  transmute(
    house,
    `z (price)` = fmt(z_price, 1),
    `z (area)` = fmt(z_area, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```
:::

## Step 3: Guess first {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-guess"}

Before we look: **rank these from strongest to weakest correlation with price.**

- Number of bedrooms
- Number of bathrooms
- Living area
- Lot (land) area
- Garage size (cars)
- Year built

## Step 3: The correlations {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-correlations"}

```{r cor-bars, fig.height = 6}
price_cor_plot(houses)
```

- Because *r* has no units, we can compare m², cars, years, and rooms on one scale.

## Step 4: Price and living area {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-step4"}

```{r price-area, fig.height = 6}
r_pa <- cor(houses$price, houses$area_m2)
price_area_plot(houses, unusual)
```

- *r* = `r fmt(r_pa, 2)`. Bigger houses sell for more, but with lots of scatter.
- House B is far off the pattern. What might be going on?

## Step 5: One coefficient {.mechanics notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-coef"}

```{r price-slope}
slope_usd_m2 <- r_pa * sd(houses$price) / sd(houses$area_m2)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
$$
z_{\text{price}} = \beta \times z_{\text{area}}
$$

- In z-scores: **β = `r fmt(r_pa, 2)`**
  - "A house 1 SD larger than average sells, on average, for `r fmt(r_pa, 2)` SD more."
- In real units: `r fmt(r_pa, 2)` × `r dollars(sd(houses$price))` /
  `r fmt(sd(houses$area_m2))` m² ≈ **`r dollars(slope_usd_m2)` per m²**
  - "Each extra square meter of living space goes with about
    `r dollars(slope_usd_m2)` more in price."
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r price-z, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
ggplot(houses, aes(z_area, z_price)) +
  geom_point(color = GRAY, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = r_pa, intercept = 0, color = ORANGE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Living area (z)", y = "Price (z)")
```
:::
:::

## Step 6: A puzzle: bedrooms {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#bedrooms-puzzle"}

```{r house-models}
house_fits <- house_models(houses)
b_alone <- house_fits[["bedrooms"]]$beta$bedrooms[1]
b_with_area <- house_fits[["bedrooms+area_m2"]]$beta$bedrooms[1]
```

```{r bedrooms-puzzle, fig.height = 5.5}
bedrooms_puzzle_plot(houses)
```

- Overall, more bedrooms go with a *higher* price (*r* = `r fmt(b_alone, 2)`).
- [But among houses of **similar size**, more bedrooms go with a *lower* price. How can
  both be true?]{.fragment}

## Step 6: Two models, two answers {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#bedrooms-solved"}

|  | price ~ bedrooms | [price ~ bedrooms + area]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |
|---|--:|--:|
| **Bedrooms** | [+`r fmt(b_alone, 2)`]{.orange} | [[`r fmt(b_with_area, 2)`]{.orange}]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |
| **Living area** |  | [+`r fmt(house_fits[["bedrooms+area_m2"]]$beta$area_m2[1], 2)`]{.fragment fragment-index=1} |

: Coefficients in SDs of price per SD of the feature

- [Big houses have more bedrooms *and* sell for more. Bedrooms alone picks up some of
  that.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
- [Hold size fixed, and an extra bedroom means smaller rooms: the sign
  flips.]{.fragment fragment-index=3}
- [Same move as height and sex: add one variable, and another's coefficient
  changes.]{.fragment fragment-index=4}

## Step 7: Every coefficient moves {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#model-builder"}

_Choose what goes into the model. Watch all the coefficients._

```{r house-models-data}
house_models_data(houses)
```

{{< include _includes/week2/model-builder.md >}}

## What to try {notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-try"}

_Four questions for the model builder on the last slide._

- **Bedrooms, then living area.** Bedrooms flips. Can you explain why, in one sentence?
- **Bathrooms, then year built.** What happens to bathrooms? What do new houses have
  more of?
- **Everything.** Which coefficient moved furthest from its correlation? Which barely
  moved?
- **The typical miss.** Which feature narrows the spread of prices the most? Which
  hardly at all?

*Which coefficient is "the" value of a bathroom? The data can't say. That's next week.*

## The model, written formally {.mechanics .smaller notes="notes/week2_notes.md#houses-model"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_{\text{price},i} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\ \sigma) && \class{blue}{\text{how prices vary around the prediction}} \\
\mu_i &= \beta_1 z_{\text{bedrooms},i} + \beta_2 z_{\text{area},i} + \dots && \class{orange}{\text{how the center moves with each feature}}
\end{aligned}
$$

| Symbol | Read it as | In the model builder |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu_i$ | the center of the price distribution for houses like house *i* | the prediction |
| $\beta_1, \beta_2, \dots$ | how far the center moves per SD of each feature, the others held fixed | the bars |
| $\sigma$ | how far prices spread around that center | the typical miss |

- Each line is a distribution: prices spread around a center ([population]{.blue}), the
  center moves with the features ([correlative]{.orange}), and every β is a number we're
  unsure about ([certainty]{.green}, the intervals).
- "The others held fixed" is why each coefficient depends on what else is in the model.
